lessons.title: Cards, actions and the pot
lessons.goal: Name your legal actions, count an additional call and build the best five cards.
lessons.recall: You face a raise to 9 after posting a big blind of 2. Explain why a call adds 7, not 9.

lessons.title: Your starting hand in context
lessons.goal: Describe position and earlier action before judging two private cards.
first_pass: Find who still has a turn
lessons.recall: Three players fold before the button at a six-player table. Name the two players who still have initial decisions.

lessons.title: Your first decisions after the flop
lessons.goal: Name a made hand and a draw separately, then read the action.
first_pass: Name the hand and the draw
lessons.recall: You hold two hearts and see two hearts on the flop. Explain why four hearts are a draw rather than a flush.

lessons.title: The turn, river and showdown
lessons.goal: Rebuild the best five after each new card and distinguish a call price from a reason to call.
lessons.recall: A river pot is 20 before a bet of 10. A call adds 10 and makes 40. Explain what 10 / 40 = 25% does and does not establish.

lessons.title: Your first range
lessons.goal: Separate known cards, possible opposing hands and assumptions about their frequency.
lessons.recall: You hold the ace of hearts. Explain why the opponent cannot hold that exact card, and why a check does not reveal their other cards.

lessons.title: Betting with a purpose
lessons.goal: Say which worse hands might call or better hands might fold, and compare betting with checking.
lessons.recall: Your bet wins when everyone folds. Explain why that ending alone does not show the bet was better than checking.

scenes.title: Before the flop: follow the seats
scenes.action: Six players start with 100 counters each. The small blind posts 1 and the big blind posts 2. There is no ante, fee or side pot. Three players fold. You are on the button, the seat marked by the dealer marker. Both blinds still have their first decisions.
scenes.question: After your initial action on the button, who still has an initial decision?
choices: Nobody; the flop must come next.
Three folds do not finish the round. Both blinds still have decisions.
The small blind and the big blind.
Yes. The two seats after the button still have their initial decisions.
Only the big blind.
The small blind still acts before the big blind. Its forced post was not its initial decision.
scenes.solution: The small blind and big blind still act. Before the flop, the initial action begins to the left of the big blind and proceeds clockwise. A raise can give earlier players another decision. The button is last in the initial order after the flop, not before it.

scenes.title: Preflop: add only what is missing
scenes.action: For this scripted practice hand, you raise to 6 total and the small blind folds. The big blind already posted 2 on this betting round and faces your total wager of 6. The current pot is your 6, the folded small blind's 1 and the big blind's 2: 9.
scenes.question: How many additional counters does the big blind need to call?
choices: 6 more.
Six is the total wager. The big blind has already paid 2 of that total on this round.
8 more.
Adding the posted 2 to the total 6 counts those forced chips twice.
4 more.
Yes. Subtract the big blind's 2 already paid from the total wager of 6.
scenes.solution: The call adds 6 - 2 = 4. The big blind's total contribution becomes 6. The pot then contains 6 + 1 + 6 = 13, and both remaining players have 94 behind. The folded small blind's counter stays in the pot. This explains the accounting, not whether either action is a good strategy.

scenes.title: The flop: name what you have now
scenes.action: The big blind calls. The flop, the first three shared cards, is jack of spades, seven of hearts and two of hearts. The big blind checks, meaning it makes no bet. Your private cards remain ace of hearts and jack of hearts.
scenes.question: Which description fits your cards on this flop?
choices: A pair of jacks and a heart-flush draw.
Yes. The two jacks make a pair; your two hearts plus two on the board make four hearts.
A completed heart flush.
A flush needs five hearts. Only four hearts are available to you now.
Only a draw, with no made hand.
The board's jack and your private jack already make a pair, even though you also have a draw.
scenes.solution: Your current best five are J-J-A-7-2. You have a pair of jacks with an ace kicker, plus four hearts among your available cards. Another heart could complete a flush, but a possible improvement is not a completed hand or a guaranteed win. After the check you can check or bet; you do not call when nothing is owed.

scenes.title: A flop raise: count this round again
scenes.action: The scripted line continues: you bet 4 and the big blind raises to 12 total on the flop. The pot is now the previous 13 plus your 4 plus the opponent's 12: 29. Your preflop contribution belongs to an earlier round.
scenes.question: How many more counters would a flop call add?
choices: 12 more.
Twelve is the opponent's total flop wager. Your 4 on this round already pays part of it.
8 more.
Yes. Match 12 total after accounting for your 4 already paid on the flop.
16 more.
The raise is to 12 total, not by another 12 on top of your bet of 4.
scenes.solution: The call adds 12 - 4 = 8, making the pot 37. Each remaining player has put in 6 preflop and 12 on the flop, leaving 82 from the original 100. You may instead fold or make a legal raise; checking is unavailable against the unmatched wager. The accounting does not establish which choice is best.

scenes.title: The river: rebuild the hand
scenes.action: You call the extra 8. The turn is nine of clubs; both players check, so nobody pays more on that round. The river is four of diamonds, the last shared card. The big blind bets 10 into the pot of 37, making the current pot 47.
scenes.question: Which statement is justified before you decide?
choices: You have a heart flush and may check.
There are still only four hearts available, and an unmatched river bet prevents checking.
Your draw can wait for one more community card.
The river is the fifth and final shared card. No later card will complete this missed draw.
You have a pair of jacks; a call would add 10.
Yes. The missed flush leaves your pair, and no earlier-round payment covers this new bet.
scenes.solution: Your best five are J-J-A-9-7. The flush did not arrive, but your pair remains. A call adds 10 and makes a final pot of 57; a fold or legal raise is also available. There is no universally correct action supplied here because the opponent's hidden hands and their frequencies have not been established.
scenes.extra: Optional after stage 4: if a call ends this heads-up cash-game hand, 10 / 57 is about 17.54%. With no fees or side pots this prices a call in chips; it does not measure your hand's equity or prove that calling is correct.

scenes.title: Showdown: separate the result and the reason
scenes.action: For the final scripted action, you call 10. The big blind reveals queen of hearts and jack of diamonds. Compare each player's best five. This is one fictional ending, not evidence about how frequently an actual opponent bluffs or bets for value.
scenes.question: Which conclusion follows from this ending?
choices: You win the pot of 57 and gain 29 overall; that result alone does not grade the earlier call.
Yes. Your ace kicker wins, and receiving the pot includes getting back your own contributions.
You make a profit of 57.
You receive 57, but 28 of it is your own earlier contribution. The net gain is 29.
Winning proves every earlier bet and call was best.
One ending does not compare your choices against the alternatives or validate an assumed range.
scenes.solution: Your J-J-A-9-7 beats the opponent's J-J-Q-9-7 because the ace kicker outranks the queen. You paid 6 + 12 + 10 = 28 and receive 57, for a net gain of 29. Your stack finishes at 129; the big blind has 72 and the folded small blind has 99. The three earlier folders still have 100 each. All six stacks sum to the original 600 counters.
